title: Your Team Needs a Cult-Like Mentality
author: Dominic Salles
summary: In this chapter of The Head of Department Manifesto, Dominic Salles argues that a team gains cohesion from a cult-like commitment to a cause and to each other, which he is careful to distinguish from an actual cult. His first lever is naming: values such as The Beats or The Steps, and techniques such as Cold Call or his own Say What You See, Say What You Need, spread faster because they are easy to say. He cites two schools that rose from requires improvement to good with branded values, and compares Doug Lemov's named techniques. His second lever is doing the team's work in public, which he says produces self-policing around an A-player standard in the manner Steve Jobs described. A thought experiment about a company of dedicated, university-educated staff who work unpaid overtime shows how much potential is wasted when teachers are left alone in closed classrooms. He supplies a ten-point team culture checklist and a Making a Difference checklist, and argues leaders need not be charismatic because teachers already share the vision of making a difference.
points: Naming values and techniques turns abstract culture into shared language, which is why a school's The Steps or Lemov's Cold Call spread so readily.
Doing the team's work in public, in shared meetings, creates self-policing norms that pull B and C players toward an A-player standard.
Teachers already share a common vision of making a difference, so the leader's task is to clear the path and not to sell a vision.
The Making a Difference checklist converts vision into curricula for what students become, what they study and what teachers study, each with measures of impact.
The ten-point team culture checklist adapts Steven Bartlett's rules toward evidence of impact, pride, mutual dependence and benchmarking against comparable departments.
quotes: We name things we value, and named things are easier to spread. This is an obvious lesson from advertising and branding.
You can see that naming these things has led to them becoming a common language that students use – not a bolt on, but a core part of the way they now think and behave.
Doug Lemov has done exactly the same thing with Teach Like a Champion: the names for his techniques make them so easy to share.
Because I have recommended doing everything in your team as a team, in public, you automatically self-police. Everyone becomes an A player, whether they started as C or B.

Your team has every one of these natural advantages, and yet, by not doing everything in public, by leaving teachers inside the closed box of their classrooms, we find so many ways to waste their potential. We start with silk and we make sows’ ears.
No one will share your vision just because you have brilliant ways of sharing it. What matters is how you harness what people already believe.
You don’t need a compelling vision. You don’t need to be a charismatic leader. You don’t need to be empathic and emotionally astute.
You need to clear a path towards the vision that your colleagues already share: to make a difference.
